formula.name: Formula
formula.def: A calculation typed into a cell. It starts with the = sign.

cell-reference.name: Cell reference
cell-reference.def: The address of a cell, such as B2 (column B, row 2).

range.name: Range
range.def: A block of cells, written like B2:B6 (from B2 down to B6).

mean.name: Mean (average)
mean.def: Add all the values, then divide by how many there are.

median.name: Median
median.def: The middle value when the numbers are put in order.

outlier.name: Outlier
outlier.def: A value far away from the others. It may be a real event or a mistake.

tolerance.name: Tolerance
tolerance.def: The allowed difference from the expected value. Real tolerances come from approved documents.

data-validation.name: Data validation
data-validation.def: A rule that only allows certain entries in a cell, such as a list or a number range.

conditional-formatting.name: Conditional formatting
conditional-formatting.def: Automatic colours that change when a cell meets a rule, such as Fail turning red.

lessons.title: Spreadsheet Basics and Formulas

cards.title: Why spreadsheets first
lines: Your work already makes numbers: readings, test results and logs.
A spreadsheet can add, compare and chart them.
It is free to start: Excel on the web or Google Sheets.

cards.title: The grid
lines: A spreadsheet is a grid of cells.
Columns have letters. Rows have numbers.
Cell B2 is column B, row 2.

cards.title: One idea per cell, one table per sheet
lines: Put one value in each cell.
Put the column name in the top row, with the unit: Time (s), Current (A).
Do not merge cells in a data table.

cards.title: A test sheet with a calculator inside
lines: A paper test sheet has boxes and columns.
A spreadsheet is the same, but it can do the sums for you.
Change one number and every result updates.

cards.title: Formulas start with =
lines: Type = and then the calculation.
Example: =2+3 gives 5.
Example: =B2*10 multiplies the value in B2 by 10.

cards.title: Five formulas to learn first
lines: They work the same in Excel and Google Sheets.

cards.title: A range
lines: B2:B6 means all cells from B2 down to B6.
Using a range lets one formula work on a whole column.

cards.title: Example (fictional data)
lines: Column A: Test number 1 to 5.
Column B: Operating time (s): 0.48, 0.50, 0.49, 0.51, 0.52.
=AVERAGE(B2:B6) gives 0.50. =MIN(B2:B6) gives 0.48. =MAX(B2:B6) gives 0.52.
These numbers are made up for practice.

cards.title: Fictional numbers only
lines: Practise with made-up numbers.
Real acceptance limits come from the manufacturer's documents and your approved procedure.
Never change a real measured value to make a sum look better.

cards.title: Practice: your first sums
lines: Open Google Sheets or Excel on the web (a computer is easier, the phone app also works).
Type the five fictional operating times in one column.
Use AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and COUNT.
Check the answers by hand.

cards.title: Recap
lines: Cells, rows, columns. One value per cell.
Formulas start with =.
SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and COUNT cover most first tasks.

quiz.q: What does every formula start with?
quiz.why: Typing = tells the spreadsheet a calculation follows.

quiz.q: What does B2:B6 mean?
options: All cells from B2 down to B6
quiz.why: A range covers a block of cells.

quiz.q: Which formula gives the mean of B2:B6?
quiz.why: AVERAGE adds the values and divides by how many there are.

quiz.q: Why put units in the column names?
quiz.why: Units prevent mistakes such as mixing seconds and milliseconds.

quiz.q: A measured value looks bad. What should you do?
options: Change it so the result passes
Keep it and find out why
quiz.why: Never change real measurements to improve results.

lessons.career: Spreadsheets are the everyday tool of testing and service work. These five formulas already save hours.

lessons.title: Tables, Filters and Sorting

cards.title: Make the table tidy first
lines: One header row at the top.
One record per row.
One kind of data per column.
No empty rows or columns inside the table.

cards.title: A tidy fictional test table
lines: Columns: Relay ID, Test, Expected (A), Measured (A), Operating time (s), Result.
Rows: one per test.
Every number has its unit in the column name.
All the data is fictional.

cards.title: Sorting
lines: Sorting puts rows in order: smallest to largest, or A to Z.
Use it to find the slowest operating time quickly.
Select the whole table before sorting, so rows stay together.

cards.title: Filtering
lines: A filter hides rows you do not need.
Show only the rows where Result is Fail.
Show only Relay R2.
Turn the filter off to see everything again.

cards.title: A pile of paper test sheets
lines: Sorting is putting the sheets in order.
Filtering is taking out only the sheets you want to read.
The other sheets are not thrown away, only hidden.

cards.title: Where to find them
lines: Menu names differ a little between tools.
In Google Sheets: Data, then Create a filter.
In Excel on the web: Data, then Filter or Sort.

cards.title: Freeze the header
lines: Freeze the top row so the column names stay visible when you scroll.
This stops you reading the wrong column.

cards.title: Keep the raw data safe
lines: Before sorting or filtering, make a copy of the original sheet.
Sorting only part of a table can mix up rows and ruin the data.
Keep the original records unchanged.

cards.title: Practice: sort and filter
lines: Make a fictional table with 10 rows and the six columns above.
Sort by operating time, largest first.
Filter to show only Fail.
Clear the filter.

cards.title: Recap
lines: Tidy table: one header, one record per row.
Sort puts rows in order. Filter hides what you do not need.
Always keep a copy of the raw data.

quiz.q: How many records should be in one row?
quiz.why: One record per row keeps tables clean.

quiz.q: What does a filter do?
options: Hides rows that do not match
quiz.why: Filtered-out rows are only hidden.

quiz.q: Why select the whole table before sorting?
options: The tool requires it for colour
quiz.why: Sorting part of a table can mix up rows.

quiz.q: What is a good first step before sorting real data?
options: Make a copy of the original
quiz.why: A copy protects the original records.

quiz.q: Why freeze the header row?
options: To keep column names visible when scrolling
quiz.why: You always see which column you are reading.

lessons.career: Finding the slow or failing tests in a long table in seconds is a daily time-saver.

lessons.title: Mean, Median, Percentage and Variation

cards.title: Why summary numbers help
lines: A table of 50 numbers is hard to read.
A few summary numbers tell the story.
We use mean, median, smallest, largest and percentage difference.

cards.title: Mean and median
lines: Mean: add all values, divide by how many.
Median: the middle value when sorted.
Use =AVERAGE(...) and =MEDIAN(...).

cards.title: Example (fictional)
lines: Now change the last value to 0.90.
Mean becomes 0.576. Median stays 0.50.
One odd value moves the mean, but hardly moves the median.

cards.title: Outliers
lines: An outlier is a value far from the others.
It may be a real event or a mistake.
Do not delete it. Find out why it happened.

cards.title: Percentage difference
lines: Percentage error = (measured minus expected) divided by expected, times 100.
The minus sign means measured is lower than expected.

cards.title: In a spreadsheet
lines: If Expected is in C2 and Measured is in D2:
Format the cell with 1 decimal place.

cards.title: Variation: how spread out
lines: MIN and MAX show the range.
Range = MAX minus MIN.
A small range means repeatable results.
Standard deviation is a more exact measure. We learn it later.

cards.title: Tolerance
lines: Tolerance is the allowed difference from the expected value.
The real tolerance comes from approved documents.
In practice tasks we use a fictional limit, such as plus or minus 5 percent.

cards.title: Maths does not decide pass or fail
lines: A formula only compares numbers.
Pass or fail uses the acceptance limits in approved documents.
If a result is close to the limit, ask a senior engineer.

cards.title: Practice: three checks
lines: Use the fictional times above.
Calculate mean, median and range.
Calculate the percentage error for expected 1.000 A and measured 1.032 A.
Check that you get 3.2 percent.

cards.title: Recap
lines: Mean and median summarise a column. Median resists odd values.
Percentage error = (measured − expected) / expected × 100.
Tolerances come from approved documents.

quiz.q: What is the median of 0.48, 0.49, 0.50, 0.51, 0.52?
quiz.why: The middle value in the ordered list is 0.50.

quiz.q: Expected 0.500 s, measured 0.485 s. What is the percentage error?
Which is less affected by one very odd value?
quiz.why: The median hardly moves when one value is extreme.

quiz.q: What should you do with an outlier?
quiz.why: An outlier may be a real event or an error. Investigate.

quiz.q: Where do real tolerances come from?
quiz.why: Real tolerances come from approved documents.

lessons.career: Percentage error and simple summaries are the first tools for reading relay test results.

lessons.title: Data Cleaning and Validation

cards.title: Messy data gives wrong answers
lines: Mixed units, typing mistakes and blank cells are common.
Clean the format before you analyse.
Clean first. Analyse second.

cards.title: Common problems
lines: Look at the table for the usual problems.

head: Problem
Example
Fix
rows: Convert to one unit and say it in the header
Use TRIM or Find and Replace
Find the record; do not guess

cards.title: Example (fictional)
lines: One tester typed 520 for operating time. Another typed 0.52.
The first is in milliseconds. The second is in seconds.
Mean of the column is meaningless until the units match.
Fix the format and write the unit in the header.

cards.title: Format fixes, not value fixes
lines: Changing a format (ms to s) is cleaning.
Changing a measured value to make it pass is falsifying data.
Never do it.

cards.title: Data validation: stop mistakes early
lines: Add a rule so a cell accepts only certain entries.
A drop-down list for Result: Pass or Fail.
A number range for Operating time: more than 0.
The tool shows a warning if the entry breaks the rule.

cards.title: Where to find it
lines: Google Sheets: Data, then Data validation.
Excel on the web: Data, then Data Validation.
Menu names vary slightly.

cards.title: Keep a record of changes
lines: Keep the original sheet unchanged.
Work on a copy.
Write a short note of what you changed and why.

cards.title: Honest data
lines: Real test records must stay true to the measurement.
If a value looks wrong, check the test and ask a senior engineer.
Never edit original records to hide a problem.

cards.title: Practice: clean a fictional table
lines: Make a small table with mixed ms and s, extra spaces and mixed spellings of Pass.
Fix each problem on a copy.
Add a drop-down for Result.
Write your list of changes.

cards.title: Recap
lines: Clean the format. Never change the measurement.
Use validation to stop errors at entry.
Work on a copy and keep notes.

quiz.q: 520 and 0.52 appear in one operating-time column. What is likely wrong?
quiz.why: One is likely milliseconds and one seconds.

quiz.q: Which is acceptable cleaning?
options: Converting ms to s and writing the unit
Changing a failing value so it passes
quiz.why: Format fixes are cleaning. Changing measurements is not.

quiz.q: What does data validation do?
options: Only allows certain entries in a cell
quiz.why: Validation rules prevent bad entries.

quiz.q: What should you do before cleaning real data?
quiz.why: A copy keeps the original safe.

quiz.q: A value looks wrong. What is the right step?
options: Check the test and ask a senior engineer
quiz.why: Investigate and escalate. Do not edit records.

resources.title: Google Sheets training and help (official, free)

lessons.career: Clean, honest data is the base of every good report and every later analysis or model.

lessons.title: Conditional Formatting and Charts

cards.title: Let colour help you read
lines: Colours make important cells easy to see.
Conditional formatting changes colour by itself when a rule is met.
Example: the word Fail turns red.

cards.title: Example (fictional)
lines: Rule 1: if Result equals Fail, colour the cell red.
Rule 2: if percentage error is more than 5 or less than −5, colour it amber.
The 5 percent is a fictional practice limit.
Real limits come from approved documents.

cards.title: Where to find it
lines: Google Sheets: Format, then Conditional formatting.
Excel on the web: Home, then Conditional Formatting.
Menu names vary slightly.

cards.title: Choosing a chart
lines: Pick the chart that answers your question.

head: Question
Chart
rows: How does a value change over tests or time?
Is one value related to another?

cards.title: A good chart
lines: A clear title.
Axis names with units.
A readable scale.
One message per chart.
Avoid 3D effects and busy colours.

cards.title: Example chart
lines: Column chart: operating time (s) for relays R1 to R5, fictional.
Add a line for the fictional upper limit.
Now anyone can see which relays are close to the limit.

cards.title: Do not mislead
lines: Start the vertical axis at a sensible value and show it clearly.
Do not cut the axis to make a small difference look big.
Label fictional data as fictional.

cards.title: Insert a chart
lines: Select the data, including the header row.
Google Sheets: Insert, then Chart.
Excel on the web: Insert, then Chart.
Then edit the title and axis names.

cards.title: Practice: colour and chart
lines: Use your fictional table.
Make Fail turn red.
Make a column chart of operating time for five relays.
Add titles and units.

cards.title: Recap
lines: Conditional formatting colours cells by rule.
Choose the chart for the question. Add titles and units.
Charts must be honest.

quiz.q: What does conditional formatting do?
options: Changes colours when a rule is met
quiz.why: It colours cells automatically by rule.

quiz.q: Which chart compares five relays?
quiz.why: Column charts compare groups.

quiz.q: What must a good chart have?
options: A title and axis names with units
quiz.why: Titles and units make a chart clear.

quiz.q: Why not cut the vertical axis to exaggerate a difference?
options: It is not allowed in Excel
quiz.why: Honest charts do not exaggerate.

quiz.q: Where do real pass or fail limits come from?
quiz.why: Colour rules only display the limits you give them.

lessons.career: A clear chart and a few colour rules can turn a table of test results into a one-glance report.
